A Simple, Interpretable Model versus a Black Box for Predicting In-Hospital Mortality in ICU Patients

707 Final Project — Final Report

Team: Junjie Cai, Yifei Chen, Jiahui Hu, Yuyao Lei

Contents: Summary · Data · Models and validation · Results · Interpretation · Limitations and conclusions · Reproducibility · References · AI statement · Supplementary materials

Summary

We compared a seven-predictor logistic generalized additive model (GAM-7) with XGBoost using a broader first-24-hour feature set (XGB-full), with additional interpretable models and clinical-score benchmarks. The outcome was in-hospital death. Model development used nested cross-validation in set A; sets B and C were held out from training and tuning.

Set A contained 4,000 records and 554 deaths (13.85%). The pooled out-of-fold AUROC was 0.736 for GAM-7 and 0.826 for XGB-full. Their paired difference was 0.091 (conditional bootstrap 95% CI 0.072 to 0.110). Brier scores were 0.109 and 0.097, respectively.

The tested compact GAM sacrificed discrimination for a simpler additive representation. This is a comparison of these fitted specifications, not proof that every interpretable model must perform worse. No equivalence margin was specified, so the study does not establish equivalence or noninferiority. Post hoc explanations help describe XGBoost's predictions; neither these explanations nor the decision curves establish clinical benefit or causal effects.

Data, predictors, and quality checks

Source and eligible cohort

We used PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2012 v1.0.0, including set-a, set-b, and set-c and their corresponding outcome files [1,2,3,5]. The unit of analysis was an ICU stay record. The source cohort required an ICU stay of at least 48 hours; therefore, this analysis does not represent all ICU admissions, including those dying or discharged before that eligibility threshold [3]. Although the source describes adult admissions, a few recorded ages are below 18; the analysis retains the supplied cohort and treats this as a data-quality limitation.

Table 1. Cohort characteristics and mortality by PhysioNet data set.

Set Records Deaths Mortality (%) Median age
A 4000 554 13.85 67.00
B 4000 568 14.20 67.00
C 4000 585 14.62 67.00

No record was excluded solely because predictors were missing. Outcome linkage was checked one-to-one by RecordID, with binary outcome coding and matching record counts. Sets B and C are same-source held-out test sets, not independent geographic or prospective external validation cohorts.

Feature construction

Predictors use measurements between 00:00 and 24:00 inclusive. Every raw record file was checked to be in chronological order, so first/last summaries follow the recorded time sequence. Negative sentinel values for static descriptors and weight, and values outside the broad plausibility ranges listed in code/01_build_features.py, are set to missing; FiO2 percentages are converted to fractions. These screens do not guarantee removal of every erroneous measurement.

The small-7 features are age, minimum GCS, mean heart rate, mean combined MAP, mean respiratory rate, minimum SaO2, and maximum BUN. Core-15 adds minimum PaO2, maximum creatinine, maximum WBC, minimum platelets, minimum hematocrit, maximum glucose, maximum bilirubin, and mean temperature. Combined MAP uses invasive measurements when available, otherwise non-invasive measurements.

The seven-variable set follows the proposal (Section 3.2): age represents demographics; GCS represents neurological status; heart rate and MAP represent hemodynamics; respiratory rate and SaO2 represent respiratory status/oxygenation; and BUN represents renal-related physiology [1,3]. This is a compact, domain-based design choice, not the first seven variables selected by a statistical ranking. The code performs no outcome-based selection of these seven variables. However, the proposal provides no formal optimization of this subset or contemporaneous selection audit beyond its stated rationale. We therefore do not claim it is the optimal seven-variable set. High respiratory-variable missingness is an important weakness of this choice.

The fifteen-variable set incorporated additional physiological and laboratory measurements, including PaO₂ to further characterize respiratory status and oxygenation; creatinine and bilirubin to assess renal and hepatic function; WBC, platelets, and hematocrit to capture inflammatory and hematological status; and glucose and temperature to reflect metabolic and physiological conditions [1,3]. Together, these variables provided a broader range of clinical information, allowing exploratory investigation of the potential benefits of incorporating additional predictors through comparison with an intermediate feature set.

The full set contains 193 input columns: four static descriptors, mean/minimum/maximum/last/count for 37 time-series variables, three combined-MAP summaries, and total urine output. In set A, 4 of these columns are constant after median imputation (MechVent_mean, MechVent_min, MechVent_max, MechVent_last). Thus, 193 is an input-column count, not a count of independent informative predictors. RecordID, the all-record last timestamp, the overall observation count, and the unused first-value summaries are excluded from the model inputs.

The proposal established the main variable groups and some aggregation examples, but did not document every final aggregation or sensitivity analysis. The last/count summaries and the additional missingness/ventilation sensitivity are reported as implementation choices, without claiming they were all fixed before outcomes were examined. The proposal is submitted unchanged rather than retrospectively rewritten to match the implementation.

Respiratory rate is missing for 72.6% of set A, including 2,405 of 2,405 records with documented ventilation. However, 498 records without documented ventilation also lack respiratory rate. Missing respiratory rate is therefore not equivalent to ventilation. A median-valued predictor may be an observed value or an imputed value; it cannot identify ventilation by itself.

A residual artifact audit flags 7 set-A records with mean invasive MAP above 200 mmHg while mean non-invasive MAP is between 40 and 120 mmHg. These are descriptive discordance flags, not validated exclusion rules. They remain in the primary analysis because the source does not identify which values should be corrected. Results may be sensitive to this choice; no robustness claim is made without an additional cleaning sensitivity analysis.

Missingness may encode treatment and measurement practices as well as patient condition. The sensitivity labeled GAM-7 + NA indicators in result files adds two missingness indicators and a ventilation predictor (10 inputs in total). It is abbreviated GAM-7 + NA/vent here. Its performance change cannot be attributed exclusively to missingness handling. Correlated physiological variables and repeated summaries remain in the full feature set; they can share or redistribute post hoc importance.

Models and validation

Model roles and figure selection

GAM-7, Tree-7, and XGB-7 use exactly the same seven constructed predictors. LASSO-15, Ridge-15, and XGB-15 use exactly the same core-15 predictors. XGB-full uses the full first-24-hour input set. The primary GAM-7 versus XGB-full comparison intentionally changes both representation and model family; the GAM-7 versus XGB-7 comparison holds the input set constant. There is no claim that all models use 15 predictors.

Table 3. Roles of the prespecified, supplementary, exploratory, and sensitivity models.

Role Models Purpose
Primary GAM-7, XGB-full Main compact/additive versus broader boosted-model comparison
Clinical benchmarks SAPS-I, SOFA Supplied clinical scores
Supplementary XGB-7 Compare model families using the same seven inputs
Exploratory Tree-7, LASSO-15, Ridge-15, XGB-15 Simple alternatives, penalty comparison, intermediate feature set
Sensitivity XGB-full native NA, GAM-7 + NA/vent Alternative missing-value handling/additional indicators

Ridge-15 assesses whether the core-15 logistic-regression results change with L2 rather than L1 regularization. XGB-15 provides an intermediate feature-set comparison between XGB-7 and XGB-full. Neither is a separate primary hypothesis.

For readability, the main ROC, calibration, and decision-curve figures show GAM-7, XGB-full, XGB-7, LASSO-15, Tree-7, and the two clinical benchmarks. Ridge-15, XGB-15, and the sensitivity models are omitted from those figures, but included in the complete performance tables in Appendix S1. Thus, some exploratory models are plotted and others are not; omission is not because XGBoost is a black box. SHAP was computed for XGB-full and XGB-7, not XGB-15. XGB-15 was evaluated in set-A cross-validation but was not refitted for B/C testing.

Fitting and tuning

  • GAM-7 uses penalized cubic splines, 10 basis functions per continuous predictor [6]. A common smoothing parameter is selected from 11 log-spaced values between 0.01 and 1,000 using inner-fold log-loss. A candidate whose fit raises an error receives a missing score and cannot be selected (scikit-learn default); convergence warnings were suppressed during fitting and were not logged.
  • Tree-7 tunes maximum depth (2, 3, 4) and minimum leaf size (25, 50, 100).
  • LASSO-15 and Ridge-15 use fold-internal standardization and tune inverse regularization strength C over 13 and 16 values, respectively.
  • XGBoost uses histogram-based boosting and 25 randomly sampled configurations per inner search, spanning learning rate, number of trees, maximum depth, child weight, row/column sampling, L2 penalty, and split penalty. The maximum searched tree count is 600. Median imputation is primary; native missing-value handling is a separate sensitivity model [7].

Set A uses stratified five-fold outer cross-validation with the same outer folds for every model (seed 707). Each outer training set has an inner stratified five-fold search (seed 708). Imputation, scaling, and tuning occur only within the relevant training folds [8]. After evaluation, selected models are tuned on all of set A and refitted for interpretation and B/C prediction; these fitted interpretation models are distinct from the outer-fold fits used for performance.

Selected configurations for each outer fold are reported in Appendix S4.

All primary fitted models, including XGB-full, use training-fold median imputation. For a shared predictor and identical training split, independently fitted imputers therefore produce the same replacement value. LASSO and Ridge add standardization after imputation. Native XGBoost missing-value routing is restricted to the explicitly labeled sensitivity model. Consequently, native versus median handling is not mixed into the primary model comparison, although the broader feature set can still contain additional missingness information through measurement counts.

Clinical scores and metrics

SAPS-I and SOFA are taken from the supplied outcomes files, with negative values treated as missing. Their raw scores are used consistently for AUROC, including paired bootstrap comparisons [9,10]. For AUPRC (average precision), Brier score, calibration, thresholds, and decision curves, scores are converted to probabilities by logistic recalibration fitted only on outer training folds. The supplied score windows were not independently reconstructed from raw measurements; their temporal comparability to our first-24-hour predictors is therefore uncertain.

Calibration-in-the-large is an intercept estimated with slope fixed at one; calibration slope is estimated with a free intercept. Thresholds are the corresponding outer training-fold mortality prevalence and 0.30. They are illustrative evaluation thresholds, not validated treatment rules.

Paired percentile bootstrap intervals use 2,000 patient resamples of fixed out-of-fold predictions, using the same eligible records for both models in each comparison. They do not capture retraining, tuning, or fold-assignment uncertainty. Exploratory comparisons are not adjusted for multiplicity.

Positive AUROC differences favor the first model; negative Brier differences favor the first model. Interval interpretation is conditional on the fitted out-of-fold predictions and should not be treated as a fully refitted cross-validation uncertainty analysis.

With seven inputs, XGB-7 achieved AUROC 0.762; XGB-15 achieved 0.786; and XGB-full achieved 0.826. These ordered feature-set comparisons suggest that the broader input representation was useful under the implemented tuning procedure. They do not isolate individual features, monitoring frequency, or interactions: feature content and fitted hyperparameters change together. The XGB-7 versus GAM-7 difference compares model specifications on the same inputs, not a pure estimate of interaction benefit. These AUROC differences must not be interpreted as a causal percentage decomposition.

Ridge-15 and LASSO-15 yielded AUROCs of 0.720 and 0.720. Their closeness is descriptive, not a formal equivalence result. The expanded GAM-7 + NA/vent sensitivity achieved 0.750; it includes information absent from GAM-7 and should not be called a pure imputation comparison.

Interpretation

Additive effects and model complexity

Table 10. Model inputs and fitted complexity.

Model Inputs Fitted complexity
Tree-7 7 depth 3, 8 leaves = 8 if-then rules
GAM-7 7 7 smooth terms, effective df = 27.9
LASSO-15 15 14 non-zero coefficients
Ridge-15 15 15 shrunken coefficients
XGB-7 7 600 trees × depth 2 (median over folds; ≤ 2,400 leaves)
XGB-15 15 600 trees × depth 4 (median over folds; ≤ 9,600 leaves)
XGB-full 193 600 trees × depth 3 (median over folds; ≤ 4,800 leaves)
SAPS-I 14 variables Fixed additive point score
SOFA 6 organ systems Fixed additive point score

Tree rules, additive smooths, and linear coefficients are directly inspectable representations. They are not automatically clinically reliable. XGBoost requires post hoc summaries; its interpretability is not equivalent to that of a small decision tree or an additive model.

These curves describe fitted associations on the development data. GCS, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation may also reflect treatment or recording practices. Sedation, surgical recovery, and clinical measurement decisions were not separately measured or tested, so they cannot be established as mechanisms from these plots. Last-value summaries describe recent observed state, not an explicit trajectory or rate of recovery.

XGBoost and SHAP

TreeExplainer was used for XGB-full and XGB-7, with model-output contributions on the log-odds scale [4,11]. Explanations are computed on the full set-A refits and are descriptive in-sample analyses, not out-of-fold explanation validation. XGB-15 has performance estimates but no SHAP analysis in this project.

The highest-ranked full-model inputs by mean absolute SHAP are GCS_last, Age, Urine_sum, BUN_last, RespRate_count, pH_count. These rankings describe attribution under the fitted model and explanation method. Correlated summaries can share attribution; a high rank does not establish a causal effect or prove that removing the feature would reduce predictive performance.

Table 12. Ten highest-ranked XGB-full predictors by mean absolute SHAP.

Feature Mean absolute SHAP
GCS_last 0.3043
Age 0.2793
Urine_sum 0.1931
BUN_last 0.1439
RespRate_count 0.1362
pH_count 0.1056
BUN_mean 0.0872
GCS_max 0.0858
Urine_last 0.0847
HR_mean 0.0829

Measurement counts can carry information about data availability and clinical practice. An ablation study would be needed to attribute performance improvement specifically to count features, last values, or any other feature family.

Partial dependence replaces one input while leaving other inputs unchanged. Because this feature set contains correlated summaries (for example minimum, maximum, mean, and last values of the same variable), this can create unrealistic combinations. These curves are model summaries, not simulated clinical interventions.

Table 13. Leading pairwise SHAP interactions for XGB-7.

Feature 1 Feature 2 Mean absolute pair contribution
MAPc_mean BUN_max 0.1188
GCS_min MAPc_mean 0.1060
Age BUN_max 0.0887
Age MAPc_mean 0.0795
Age GCS_min 0.0743

GCS_min BUN_max 0.0353
Age HR_mean 0.0313
MAPc_mean RespRate_mean 0.0278

The pair statistic is twice the mean absolute off-diagonal SHAP interaction value, counting both symmetric entries. It is an attribution-magnitude summary, not a percentage of model performance. Absolute main-effect and total-SHAP magnitudes cannot be divided into a valid percentage of signal explained: signed contributions can cancel, and absolute values are not additive. The project therefore makes no claim that an additive model captures a particular percentage of the full signal.

Limitations and conclusions

The comparison is limited by a single retrospective data source, a cohort selected to have ICU stays of at least 48 hours, substantial missingness, residual measurement artifacts, and uncertainty about supplied clinical-score windows. No alternate MAP-cleaning analysis or feature-family ablation was performed. Native missing-value handling and added indicators address only part of these issues.

The tuning search is finite. Selecting the maximum searched number of trees indicates a search boundary, not evidence that increasing it must improve performance or strengthen the conclusion. Other compact model specifications, feature selections, and tuning ranges could give different comparisons. Bootstrap intervals condition on existing predictions; repeated nested cross-validation or full refitting would be needed to assess additional training variability. Multiple exploratory comparisons and in-sample explanation plots should be interpreted accordingly.

Within the tested specifications, XGB-full offers better discrimination and probability accuracy than GAM-7, while GAM-7 offers a simpler additive representation. The seven-input and core-15 XGBoost comparisons provide context for this trade-off, without identifying a causal source of the gain. Neither predictive performance nor post hoc interpretability establishes that a model is ready for clinical deployment.

Reproducibility and project organization

The analysis is a sequence of numbered Python scripts in code/, run in the order 01 → 02 → 03 → 05 by run_all.sh:

Script Purpose
01_build_features.py Parse raw records and build first-24-hour features for sets A, B, and C
02_data_quality.py Cohort summary, missingness, distributions, redundancy
03_models.py Nested cross-validation, paired bootstrap, B/C evaluation, SHAP/PDP
05_supplement.py Ridge-15, model-complexity summary
featuresets.py Shared definitions of the small-7, core-15, and full feature sets

The Python environment is specified in environment.yml (conda environment icu707). With the PhysioNet files in data/ (see README.md):

  • bash run_all.sh: extract data, build features, fit and evaluate all models, and write every table and figure to results/.
  • python code/07_final_report.py: generate this report (Final_Report.md, and a self-contained Final_Report.html when the markdown package is installed) from results/. It only reads saved results; it does not refit models.
  • python code/07_final_report.py --with-code: additionally append the analysis source code as an appendix.

run_all.sh runs the report step automatically at the end. All paths are relative to the project root. code/04_report.py and code/06_report_zh.py produce quick-look HTML summaries and are not part of this report.

Recorded modeling versions: xgboost 3.4.2; pygam 0.12.0; shap 0.51.0; sklearn 1.9.1.

AI Statement

AI tools were used to support proposal organization, code development and debugging, and the preparation of the final report and presentation. Our team established the research question, study design, predictor sets, modeling approaches, validation strategy, and evaluation metrics. AI assistance was primarily used to refine the organization of the proposal, facilitate programming, improve the clarity of written materials, and synthesize key findings for presentation. The team was also responsible for defining the analytical objectives and workflow, reviewing the implementation, and interpreting the final results.

The use of AI offered several practical advantages. In particular, AI-assisted programming improved efficiency by helping identify potential sources of coding errors, suggesting alternative debugging strategies, and accelerating the development and refinement of analytical code. AI also facilitated the communication of complex results by helping condense the detailed report into a more focused presentation narrative. Nevertheless, the project also highlighted important limitations of AI assistance. AI-generated code and explanations were not always fully consistent with the intended analytical workflow and could contain errors or rely on assumptions that were inappropriate for the collaborative computational environment. In addition, AI could oversimplify methodological concepts, overlook important analytical details, or produce interpretations that were not fully supported by the numerical results.

Overall, AI tools helped reduce the time required for structural organization, programming and debugging, and scientific writing. This allowed our team to devote greater attention to evaluating analytical decisions, understanding the underlying statistical methods, and critically interpreting the results. The team retained responsibility for all methodological decisions, analyses, and conclusions presented in this report.

Supplementary Materials / Appendix

These materials are part of the report. Tables are generated from the same result files as the main text; no additional models are fitted here. S1-S3 provide complete results, while S4 documents the selected tuning configurations. The optional analysis-code listing follows these materials only when the report is generated with --with-code.

S4. Tuning selections and numerical checks

The tables below list the configuration selected separately within each outer training fold. Fold labels 1-5 correspond to stored fold indices 0-4. Selection uses five-fold inner cross-validation and negative log-loss; all models share the outer folds. These are outer-fold selections, not the parameters of the separate full-set-A refits used for interpretation and B/C prediction.

The search ranges are described in the Methods. For XGBoost, the tables report the chosen configuration among 25 sampled configurations, not an exhaustive search of all parameter combinations.

Numerical checks. A tuning candidate whose fit raised an error received a missing cross-validation score and could not be selected (scikit-learn default). Convergence warnings were suppressed during fitting and candidate-level scores were not saved, so the number of failed candidates is not reported.
